methodContract.name: Recursive LEGO Calculus R2.1
methodContract.problem: Which AI-infrastructure constraints are binding, how fast can intelligence/automation relax them, and where does the frontier migrate next?

principles: Do not collapse technology readiness, manufacturing readiness, installed stock, annual flow, qualification and deliverability into one capacity number.
Do not scalarize heterogeneous constraints into an overall score; preserve a headroom vector and an explicit evidence-bounded minimal frontier.
Algorithmic efficiency and physical-capacity growth are separate from demand/rebound growth; lower unit cost does not imply lower total resource demand.
A global supply-chain bottleneck is not automatically a jurisdiction-specific frontier; preserve UNKNOWN when local evidence is missing.
Technology truth does not imply asset-pricing truth, investment recommendation, owner risk appetite or financial effect authority.

aggregationPolicy.quantitativeHeadroomRule: Only compute a ratio when capacity and requirement share the same unit, scope and time basis.

evidence.title: Epoch AI Huawei roadmap and 2026 compute-output model
evidence.claimBoundary: Model-based estimates: Huawei 2026 median 1.5M Ascend units / 0.88M H100e; Nvidia 5.9M chips / 23M H100e; H100e is a peak-compute normalization, not realized workload performance.

evidence.title: China AI chipmakers raise prices as HBM shortage bites
evidence.claimBoundary: Reports HBM shortage and export-control pressure raising Chinese accelerator prices; does not measure total domestic HBM capacity.

evidence.title: Samsung says HBM approaches 30% of industry DRAM wafer capacity in 2027
evidence.claimBoundary: Samsung executive says HBM is about 20% of industry DRAM wafer capacity now and nearly 30% next year; this is industry-wide, not a country stock measure.

evidence.title: SK hynix CEO expects severe memory shortage in 2027
evidence.claimBoundary: Executive view that memory demand may outstrip supply beyond 2030; forward-looking company assessment, not independent capacity measurement.

evidence.title: TrendForce AI supply-chain arms race and advanced packaging constraints
evidence.claimBoundary: Industry research reports persistent CoWoS/2.5D packaging tightness and expects TSMC CoWoS capacity to expand >60% by 2027, with severe shortage beginning to ease in 2027.

evidence.title: TrendForce CoWoS-L expected to remain mainstream through 2028
evidence.claimBoundary: Industry research says packaging demand remains strong; CoWoS-L maturity/yield support continued dominance through 2028. Not a China-specific capacity census.

evidence.title: Epoch AI Data Centers database
evidence.claimBoundary: 92 tracked large AI sites total 13.7M H100e and 13.2 GW IT power; coverage is partial and strongest for large sites.

evidence.title: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model
evidence.claimBoundary: Bottom-up model estimates China >24 GW data-center fleet at 2026YE, ~20 GW dated pipeline, ~30 GW announced; US global model 56 GW at 2026YE. These are modeled facility capacities, not AI-only energized IT load.

evidence.title: EIA planned U.S. utility-scale capacity additions for 2026
evidence.claimBoundary: EIA reports 86 GW planned utility-scale generating-capacity additions in 2026 versus 53 GW added in 2025; planned additions are not guaranteed realized firm capacity.

evidence.title: China NEA Jan-Jul 2026 power statistics
evidence.claimBoundary: China NEA reports 4.08 TW installed generation capacity at end-July 2026 and ~194 GW additions in Jan-Jul; nameplate capacity is not firm deliverable power to any specific AI site.

evidence.title: China NEA H1 2026 electricity-use briefing
evidence.claimBoundary: Internet data services consumed 49.4 TWh in H1 2026, +44% YoY; sector category is broader than AI data centers.

evidence.title: 2026 China Computing Power Conference capacity snapshot
evidence.claimBoundary: Reports 15.56M standard racks, 2,185 EFLOPS FP16 intelligent compute and >2,000 EB storage as of June 2026; standard racks and FP16 aggregates are not directly comparable to frontier H100e deployment.

evidence.title: U.S. utilities scramble for transformers and switchgear
evidence.claimBoundary: Reports some high-voltage transformer lead times up to 160 weeks and equipment cost increases up to 10%; lead times vary by specification and supplier.

evidence.title: China transformer exports and AI/grid demand
evidence.claimBoundary: Reports H1 transformer exports CNY39.792B, +26.78% YoY; >10 MVA liquid transformer exports +50%. Export growth does not prove absence of domestic local bottlenecks.

evidence.title: Berkeley Lab Queued Up 2026
evidence.claimBoundary: At end-2025 >2,060 GW generation+storage sought U.S. interconnection; most projects historically withdraw and timelines remain long. Queue volume is not realizable capacity.

evidence.title: DOE smart transmission tools and Dynamic Line Rating
evidence.claimBoundary: DOE/INL research found DLR can increase transfer capability by roughly 10-40% in suitable conditions; it cannot remove conductor, substation, stability or siting limits.

evidence.title: China NEA summer 2026 grid and UHV capacity briefing
evidence.claimBoundary: Reports 46 operating UHV corridors and >340 GW west-to-east transfer capability; national transfer capability does not guarantee local AI-site interconnection headroom.

evidence.title: IEA Energy and AI data-center demand scenarios
evidence.claimBoundary: IEA Base Case projects global data-center electricity consumption near 945 TWh in 2030 and emphasizes 2-3 year data-center build times versus longer energy-system lead times. Scenario, not forecast certainty.

evidence.title: NIST 2026 AI/ML for Smart Manufacturing roadmap
evidence.claimBoundary: Identifies AI opportunities in sensing, autonomous systems, digital twins, robotics, logistics and manufacturing while retaining integration, reliability and trustworthy-operation barriers.

nodes.label: Frontier AI accelerator logic and delivered compute

ceilings: wafer capacity, process equipment, yield and packaging still require physical throughput
software efficiency cannot create unavailable dies

readiness.reason: This node aggregates multiple commercial accelerator generations and process routes; TRL/MRL must be attached to a specific device/process, not the layer.

ceilings: wafer starts, TSV/stacking, packaging equipment and qualification are physical
HBM and commodity DRAM compete for wafer capacity

readiness.reason: HBM generations are commercial but capacity/yield/qualification differ by vendor and generation; one aggregate TRL/MRL would be misleading.

ceilings: qualified packaging lines, substrates, bonding/TSV equipment and yield ramp remain physical
larger interposers increase material and process burden

readiness.reason: CoWoS/EMIB/other technologies have different maturity and capacity; the graph tracks the supply layer, not a single package technology.

nodes.label: AI-ready data-center IT and electrical capacity

ceilings: land, switchgear, substations, construction and commissioning still consume calendar time
generic data-center MW is not automatically high-density liquid-cooled AI MW

readiness.reason: The node is an installed-capacity layer composed of many mature technologies; readiness is site-specific.

mechanisms: forecasting, dispatch, siting and maintenance optimization
demand shaping can improve effective use of existing generation
ceilings: new generation requires equipment, fuel/resource access, construction, interconnection and permits
nameplate MW is not equivalent to firm power at a specific site

readiness.reason: Generation is a portfolio of mature and emerging technologies; technology-specific readiness must remain separate.

mechanisms: factory scheduling, inspection and predictive quality
ceilings: copper, electrical steel, winding/drying/test equipment and factory slots cannot be copied like software
high-voltage equipment must pass qualification and commissioning

readiness.reason: Conventional equipment is mature, while solid-state variants are emerging; the active issue is throughput and delivery, not a single readiness level.

mechanisms: dynamic line ratings and topology optimization
ceilings: rights-of-way, substations, stability, conductors and new corridors remain physical/institutional
software can unlock stranded capacity but cannot remove hard thermal and reliability limits

readiness.reason: Grid deliverability mixes mature hardware, operating methods and permitting institutions; readiness is use-case-specific.

edges.assumption: Most frontier accelerators require high-bandwidth memory; non-HBM designs are a separate substitution path and must be modeled explicitly.
High-performance HBM systems require qualified packaging/integration; memory availability alone does not create a deployable accelerator.
Packaged accelerators require servers, networking, cooling and powered AI-ready IT capacity.
Nominal IT MW must be served over time; energy source and firmness are separate from rack nameplate capacity.
Generation cannot serve the load without appropriate transformers, switchgear and substation equipment.
Equipment at a site is insufficient without an admitted interconnection/transmission path or an explicitly separate behind-the-meter architecture.

headroom.reason: Leading U.S.-ecosystem accelerator suppliers are shipping rapidly growing compute; current public evidence points to downstream complements becoming more binding than accelerator design/supply at the ecosystem level.

assumptions: Global Nvidia supply is a proxy for the U.S.-led ecosystem, not U.S.-domestic ownership or deployed capacity.
reopenConditions: Material delivery cuts or allocation shortages re-emerge despite downstream capacity availability.
A major export/supply shock removes a large fraction of usable accelerator flow.

headroom.reason: HBM remains sold/tight enough that vendors are reallocating DRAM wafer capacity toward it; however it is not uniquely U.S.-specific and large capacity expansion is underway.

assumptions: U.S. AI builders retain access to leading Korean/U.S. HBM supply subject to commercial allocation.
reopenConditions: HBM allocation or qualification delays become the dominant reason energized U.S. capacity cannot accept accelerators.
Capacity ramps materially ahead of accelerator demand and allocation constraints disappear.

headroom.reason: CoWoS/2.5D packaging remains a global constrained complement, but announced expansion and alternatives are expected to reduce severity beginning around 2027.

assumptions: U.S. accelerator supply remains substantially dependent on Asian advanced-packaging capacity.
reopenConditions: Packaging wait times, pricing or allocation become the dominant limiter after HBM/logic are available.
New CoWoS/EMIB/OSAT capacity removes backlog faster than accelerator demand grows.

headroom.reason: Large AI-ready sites are expanding quickly, but AI-ready powered capacity is location-specific and cannot be inferred from all data-center MW.

assumptions: All-data-center capacity is not equivalent to high-density AI IT capacity.
reopenConditions: Powered AI-ready capacity becomes broadly available faster than chip deployments.
Regional power/MEP delays prevent otherwise-financed accelerators from being installed.

headroom.reason: The U.S. is adding record utility-scale capacity, but local firm power and data-center timing can still bind; national nameplate additions do not settle site-level deliverability.

assumptions: Planned utility-scale additions include variable renewables and storage; firm capacity contribution differs by technology and region.
reopenConditions: Data-center load growth persistently exceeds locally deliverable firm generation despite grid/equipment availability.
Generation additions and load flexibility remove local energy constraints while equipment/grid queues remain.

headroom.reason: High-voltage transformers, breakers and switchgear have multi-year lead times and utilities are ordering years ahead; this is direct physical throughput evidence.

assumptions: Reported lead times vary materially by voltage, specification and supplier.
reopenConditions: Lead times fall materially and remain low across multiple voltage classes while data-center orders continue rising.
Utilities/developers identify a different component as the dominant schedule blocker.

headroom.reason: U.S. generation/storage interconnection queues remain enormous and process timelines long; grid-delivery constraints can prevent nominal generation from reaching new load.

assumptions: Queue MW is not realizable supply; high withdrawal rates mean it is primarily evidence of process congestion and project interest.
reopenConditions: Median interconnection study/energization timelines fall materially and queue completion rates rise.
Behind-the-meter architectures bypass the grid for a large fraction of incremental AI load without introducing a new turbine/fuel bottleneck.

headroom.reason: China can build data centers and power infrastructure faster than it can currently supply frontier-equivalent domestic compute; export controls and domestic per-chip/output gaps make accelerator logic a direct frontier.

assumptions: Epoch figures are model estimates and H100e is an on-paper peak-compute normalization, not realized workload throughput.
reopenConditions: Domestic delivered compute output rises enough that powered AI-ready capacity rather than accelerator supply becomes the repeated schedule limiter.
Access to leading external accelerators materially reopens and remains durable.

headroom.reason: China-specific HBM scarcity is directly showing through accelerator pricing and memory sourcing constraints; domestic HBM-supported frontier output remains materially smaller than total accelerator plans.

assumptions: The 240k estimate is model-based and vendor-specific; it is not total China HBM production.
reopenConditions: Domestic HBM volume/yield/qualification expands enough that accelerator pricing and shipments are no longer memory-constrained.
Export-control or grey-market availability materially changes HBM access.

headroom.reason: Advanced packaging is globally tight and structurally necessary, but this R1 evidence set lacks a sufficiently direct China-specific capacity/current-backlog measure to call it a current frontier independently of logic/HBM.

assumptions: Global CoWoS scarcity is not automatically evidence of the exact domestic China packaging frontier.
reopenConditions: Obtain China-specific 2.5D/3D qualified capacity, backlog, yield and customer-qualification evidence.
Provider/industry evidence shows packaging—not logic/HBM—is the dominant lost-output constraint.

headroom.reason: China has a large existing data-center fleet and substantial dated pipeline; current evidence does not support national AI-ready shell capacity as the primary constraint, though retrofit/high-density site quality remains heterogeneous.

assumptions: Generic data-center GW and standard racks do not prove high-density accelerator-ready power/cooling quality.
reopenConditions: High-density AI-ready utilization/backlog data show persistent national shortage despite available shells.
Accelerator/HBM constraints ease and data-center energization becomes the dominant schedule limiter.

headroom.reason: National generation stock and additions are very large relative to current AI load; evidence supports substantial aggregate power headroom, while site-level firm power may still be constrained.

assumptions: Installed/nameplate generation is not equivalent to firm deliverable MW at each data-center location.
reopenConditions: AI/data-center load growth creates repeated firm-power rationing at major compute hubs.
Grid/equipment constraints become resolved but energy availability remains the dominant limiter.

headroom.reason: China's transformer industry is expanding domestic and export output; public evidence does not show a U.S.-style national equipment bottleneck, though local/project-specific queues remain possible.

assumptions: Export growth is not direct measurement of domestic spare capacity or AI-specific equipment lead time.
reopenConditions: Domestic lead times lengthen persistently across major voltage classes and become a repeated AI-project blocker.
Export growth reverses because domestic demand absorbs available production.

headroom.reason: China has very large long-distance grid transfer infrastructure; national evidence does not support grid capacity as the primary AI bottleneck today, while regional congestion and renewable-firming remain real subproblems.

assumptions: National transfer capability is not local interconnection headroom for a particular data center.
reopenConditions: Regional AI clusters experience persistent connection delays despite available accelerator supply.
Transmission congestion/curtailment becomes the dominant constraint on delivered AI electricity.

assumptions: Useful-work demand doubles while useful-work-per-unit-compute triples.
No independent workload-quality or latency requirement offsets the efficiency gain.
falsifiers: Inference-time scaling or agent duration increases required compute more than the assumed demand multiplier.
Efficiency improvements fail to transfer to the dominant production workloads.

assumptions: Cheaper/more capable AI expands agent-hours, inference depth and applications tenfold while efficiency triples.
Supply-side substitution does not eliminate the listed complements.
falsifiers: Economic utilization saturates and demand grows less than efficiency.
A new architecture sharply reduces dependence on one or more listed complements.
